idiom_name: Range with (..)/(...), endless/beginless forms, cover? and overlap?
implementation_notes: Ruby's Range is a core class that already carries the pattern: (1..5) is closed, (1...5) excludes the upper bound, (1..) and (..5) are endless/beginless (open-ended by construction), cover? answers membership with comparison semantics suitable for non-numeric types, and === makes a range usable in case/when. Ruby 3.3 added Range#overlap? (feature #19839), so overlap is stdlib too, and it returns false for empty ranges or incomparable endpoints instead of raising. What remains hand-written is interval-to-interval intersection/span, a canonical empty range, and any enumeration at all for an endless range - (1..) is not enumerable, so loops must stay bounded.
code_sketch:
billing = Date.new(2026, 1, 1)...Date.new(2026, 4, 1)   # half-open
billing.cover?(Date.new(2026, 2, 15))                  # => true
billing.overlap?(previous_period)                      # Ruby 3.3+

valued = 1..                                           # endless range (no loop!)

# intersection is still hand-written:
lo = [a.begin, b.begin].max
hi = [a.end, b.end].min   # then adjust for an exclusive end
pitfalls: cover? and include? differ outside numerics: for a Date range include? enumerates while cover? compares, so use cover? (or ===) for membership tests over time ranges.
(1...1) has begin == end but is empty, while (1..1) contains exactly 1: the exclusive flag is the whole distinction, and Range#to_a on an endless range raises.

Range#overlap? returns false when either range is empty and also when the endpoints are incomparable (<=> returns nil), so mixing a Date range with a Time boundary answers false instead of failing loudly.
Endless and beginless ranges cannot be enumerated or reversed, and Range#last raises on them; any method that iterates must be guarded by a bounded range.
